Set a random seed before each simulation question and report it. You may use standard packages unless a question asks you to write the calculation yourself. Use equal neighbor weights throughout. Here pp counts the covariates used to measure distance; do not add an intercept column to a KNN predictor matrix. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact simulation results need not agree.

Question 1: Estimate the bias and variance of KNN

In our previous homework, we used repeated simulations to study the behavior of linear regression estimators. We will now use the same idea for KNN. Consider the regression model

Yi=f(𝐗i)+ϵi,f(𝐱)=0.5x1+sin(x2)−0.3x32, Y_i=f(\mathbf X_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad f(\mathbf x)=0.5x_1+\sin(x_2)-0.3x_3^2,

where the three covariates are independent standard normal variables and ϵi∼𝒩(0,0.12)\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2) independently of the covariates and other observations. Generate n=400n=400 training observations. Our goal is to estimate the mean response at

𝐱0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Use Euclidean distance and consider k=1,3,5,…,29k=1,3,5,\ldots,29.

  1. Calculate f(𝐱0)f(\mathbf x_0). Generate one training dataset and obtain the KNN prediction at 𝐱0\mathbf x_0 for each value of kk.

  2. Independently repeat the generation of the training covariates and responses 200 times. Within each repetition, use the same training data for every value of kk. Store the predictions in a matrix with 200 rows and one column for each value of kk. Use this matrix to estimate the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the estimated mean response. Use divisor 200 when calculating the empirical variance, and verify numerically that

mean squared error=squared bias+variance. \text{mean squared error} =\text{squared bias}+\text{variance}.

Plot squared bias, variance, and mean squared error against kk in one figure. Explain the pattern and compare it with the bias-variance trade-off for ridge regression or lasso.

Solution: Question 1

Show the workflow 
set.seed(432)

x0 <- c(0.5, 0.7, 1)

f_x0 <- 0.5 * x0[1] + sin(x0[2]) - 0.3 * x0[3]^2

n <- 400

X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), nrow = n, ncol = 3)

epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.1)

y <- 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2 + epsilon

distances <- sqrt(rowSums((X - matrix(x0, nrow = n, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE))^2))

neighbor_order <- order(distances)

k_values <- seq(1, 29, by = 2)

knn_predictions <- sapply(k_values, function(k) {
  neighbors <- neighbor_order[1:k]
  mean(y[neighbors])
})

B <- 200

predictions <- matrix(NA, nrow = B, ncol = length(k_values))

for (b in 1:B) {
  
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), nrow = n, ncol = 3)
  
  epsilon <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.1)
  
  y <- 0.5 * X[, 1] +
    sin(X[, 2]) -
    0.3 * X[, 3]^2 +
    epsilon
  
  distances <- sqrt(
    rowSums((X - matrix(x0, nrow = n, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE))^2)
  )
  
  neighbor_order <- order(distances)
  
  predictions[b, ] <- sapply(k_values, function(k) {
    neighbors <- neighbor_order[1:k]
    mean(y[neighbors])
  })
}

mean_predictions <- colMeans(predictions)

bias <- mean_predictions - f_x0

f(x0)=0.5942f(x_0) = 0.5942

The estimated MSE was approximately equal to the squared bias plus the variance for each value of k. This confirms the bias-variance decomposition using the 200 simulated training sets. As k increases, the variance decreases because the prediction is based on more observations. At the same time, the squared bias generally increases because larger values of k include observations that are farther away from x0x_0. This creates a bias-variance tradeoff, which is why the MSE is lowest somewhere in the middle. This is similar to ridge and lasso because increasing the penalty makes the model less flexible, which generally decreases variance but increases bias.

Question 2: Compare KNN with lasso

Use the response model from Question 1, including the noise standard deviation 0.10.1, but generate p=30p=30 covariates. The response still depends only on the first three. Consider these two settings:

  • Setting 1: all 30 covariates are independent standard normal variables.

  • Setting 2: the covariates have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, where

    Σjj=1,Σjl=0.8for j≠l. \Sigma_{jj}=1, \qquad \Sigma_{jl}=0.8\quad\text{for }j\ne l.

In each setting, generate 400 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations. Fit 5NN using Euclidean distance on the supplied covariate scale. All covariates already have population variance one.

For lasso, use a linear model containing the 30 covariates and a separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Follow the Week 4 objective,

Lλ(𝛃)=12n∥𝐲̃−𝐗𝛃∥22+λ‖𝛃‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 +\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝐗∈ℝn×30\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times30} contains the centered and standardized covariates and 𝐲̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered training response. Select the penalty by ten-fold cross-validation over 41 logarithmically spaced values from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Estimate all means and scales using only the training portion of each fold, with divisor equal to that portion’s sample size. After selecting the penalty, refit on all training observations and apply the fitted transformations unchanged to the test observations. Do not add nonlinear terms to the lasso model.

  1. Fit both methods in each setting. Use the same training and test data for the two methods within a setting. Report their test MSE values in one table, together with the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero lasso slopes. You only need to generate one dataset for each setting; repeated simulations are not required.

  2. Compare the results between the two settings. Explain how correlation can change the usefulness of Euclidean neighborhoods, and why lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN.

  3. The response model contains sin(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso fit uses only linear terms. Explain how this difference affects the comparison. Would the results justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN, or that one method is always better? Explain why.

Solution: Question 2

Show the workflow 
set.seed(432)

library(FNN)
library(glmnet)
Warning: package 'glmnet' was built under R version 4.5.2
Loading required package: Matrix

Attaching package: 'Matrix'
The following objects are masked from 'package:tidyr':

    expand, pack, unpack
Loaded glmnet 5.1
Show the workflow 
n <- 400
p <- 30
lambda <- 10^seq(0, -4, length.out = 41)

results <- data.frame(
  Setting = c("Independent", "Correlated"),
  KNN_MSE = NA_real_,
  Lasso_MSE = NA_real_,
  Lambda = NA_real_,
  Nonzero = NA_integer_
)

for (l in 1:2) {
  
  Sigma <- diag(p)
  
  if (l == 2) {
    Sigma <- 0.8 + 0.2 * diag(p)
  }
  
  X <- matrix(rnorm((n + 1000) * p), ncol = p) %*% chol(Sigma)
  
  y <- 0.5 * X[, 1] +
    sin(X[, 2]) -
    0.3 * X[, 3]^2 +
    rnorm(n + 1000, sd = 0.1)
  
  test.X <- X[(n + 1):(n + 1000), ]
  test.y <- y[(n + 1):(n + 1000)]
  
  X <- X[1:n, ]
  y <- y[1:n]
  
  knn.fit <- knn.reg(
    X,
    test.X,
    y,
    k = 5,
    algorithm = "brute"
  )
  
  results$KNN_MSE[l] <- mean(
    (test.y - knn.fit$pred)^2
  )
  
  fold <- sample(rep(1:10, each = n / 10))
  
  cv.mse <- matrix(
    NA_real_,
    nrow = 10,
    ncol = length(lambda)
  )
  
  for (m in 1:10) {
    
    X.mean <- colMeans(X[fold != m, ])
    
    X.fit <- sweep(
      X[fold != m, ],
      2,
      X.mean,
      "-"
    )
    
    X.sd <- sqrt(colMeans(X.fit^2))
    
    X.fit <- sweep(
      X.fit,
      2,
      X.sd,
      "/"
    )
    
    X.valid <- sweep(
      X[fold == m, ],
      2,
      X.mean,
      "-"
    )
    
    X.valid <- sweep(
      X.valid,
      2,
      X.sd,
      "/"
    )
    
    y.mean <- mean(y[fold != m])
    
    lasso.fit <- glmnet(
      X.fit,
      y[fold != m] - y.mean,
      alpha = 1,
      lambda = lambda,
      intercept = FALSE,
      standardize = FALSE
    )
    
    y.hat <- predict(
      lasso.fit,
      newx = X.valid,
      s = lambda
    ) + y.mean
    
    cv.mse[m, ] <- colMeans(
      (y[fold == m] - y.hat)^2
    )
  }
  
  lambda.min <- lambda[
    which.min(colMeans(cv.mse))
  ]
  
  X.mean <- colMeans(X)
  
  X.fit <- sweep(
    X,
    2,
    X.mean,
    "-"
  )
  
  X.sd <- sqrt(colMeans(X.fit^2))
  
  X.fit <- sweep(
    X.fit,
    2,
    X.sd,
    "/"
  )
  
  test.X.fit <- sweep(
    test.X,
    2,
    X.mean,
    "-"
  )
  
  test.X.fit <- sweep(
    test.X.fit,
    2,
    X.sd,
    "/"
  )
  
  y.mean <- mean(y)
  
  lasso.fit <- glmnet(
    X.fit,
    y - y.mean,
    alpha = 1,
    lambda = lambda,
    intercept = FALSE,
    standardize = FALSE
  )
  
  test.pred <- as.vector(
    predict(
      lasso.fit,
      newx = test.X.fit,
      s = lambda.min
    )
  ) + y.mean
  
  results$Lasso_MSE[l] <- mean(
    (test.y - test.pred)^2
  )
  
  results$Lambda[l] <- lambda.min
  
  results$Nonzero[l] <- sum(
    coef(lasso.fit, s = lambda.min)[-1, 1] != 0
  )
}

results
      Setting   KNN_MSE Lasso_MSE     Lambda Nonzero
1 Independent 0.5893325 0.2393865 0.02511886      10
2  Correlated 0.1794839 0.2660958 0.02511886       5

For the independent setting, 5NN had a test MSE of 0.5893, while lasso had a test MSE of 0.2394. The selected value of λ\lambda was 0.0251, and the lasso model had 10 nonzero slopes. For the correlated setting, 5NN had a test MSE of 0.1795, while lasso had a test MSE of 0.2661. The selected value of λ\lambda was again 0.0251, and the lasso model had 5 nonzero slopes.

5NN performed much better when the predictors were correlated, with its test MSE decreasing from 0.5893 to 0.1795. When the predictors are independent, KNN has to calculate distances using all 30 dimensions, even though only the first three predictors directly affect the response. When the predictors are highly correlated, there is less unique information across the 30 dimensions, so the data effectively behaves like it has a lower dimension. This makes the distances between observations more meaningful for KNN. Lasso performed slightly worse in the correlated setting, and it also selected fewer nonzero slopes.

The true response is nonlinear because it includes sin(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, while the lasso model only includes linear terms. This puts lasso at a disadvantage because it cannot directly represent the true relationship. KNN does not assume a linear relationship, so it can better capture this nonlinearity when distances between observations are meaningful. However, these results do not mean that correlated predictors will always improve KNN or that KNN will always perform better than lasso. The performance of each method depends on factors such as the relationship between the predictors and response, the number of predictors, and the correlation structure.

Question 3: Observed dimension and latent dimension

The lecture’s handwritten digit example shows that KNN can work with many measured covariates. We will use a simulation to investigate why the structure of those covariates matters.

Let p=100p=100 be the number of observed covariates and let mm be the number of latent variables. For each observation, generate

𝐗i=𝐀𝐙i+𝛈i,Yi=Zi1+Zi2+ϵi, \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i+\boldsymbol\eta_i, \qquad Y_i=Z_{i1}+Z_{i2}+\epsilon_i,

where 𝐀∈ℝ100×m\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{100\times m} has independent entries from Uniform[−2,2][-2,2]. The entries of 𝐙i∈ℝm\mathbf Z_i\in\mathbb R^m and 𝛈i∈ℝ100\boldsymbol\eta_i\in\mathbb R^{100}, and the scalar ϵi\epsilon_i, are independent standard normal variables, also independent of 𝐀\mathbf A. Generate 𝐀\mathbf A once and use it for all training and test observations in that dataset.

Compare m=3m=3 and m=30m=30. In each setting, generate 200 training observations and 200 independent test observations. Fit KNN using only the 100 observed covariates in 𝐗\mathbf X, with Euclidean distance on their generated scale. The latent variables in 𝐙\mathbf Z are used to generate the data but are not available to the fitted model. Consider k=2,10,18,…,82k=2,10,18,\ldots,82.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of mm. Fit KNN for every value of kk and calculate test MSE. Within a setting, use the same training and test observations for all values of kk.

  2. Repeat the complete experiment 50 times, generating a new 𝐀\mathbf A and new observations in each repetition. Plot average test MSE against kk, with one curve for each value of mm. These curves compare the specified choices of kk in a controlled simulation; they are not a cross-validation procedure for selecting a final model.

  3. Both settings have 100 observed covariates, and the response depends on only two latent variables. Explain why their KNN performance can still differ. What role does the noise 𝛈i\boldsymbol\eta_i play, and why are the observed data not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space?

Solution: Question 3

Show the workflow 
set.seed(432)

library(FNN)

p <- 100
m_values <- c(3, 30)
k_values <- seq(2, 82, by = 8)

test_mse <- matrix(
  NA,
  nrow = length(k_values),
  ncol = length(m_values)
)

for (j in seq_along(m_values)) {
  
  m <- m_values[j]
  
  A <- matrix(rnorm(p * m), nrow = p, ncol = m)
  
  Z <- matrix(rnorm(400 * m), nrow = 400, ncol = m)
  
  eta <- matrix(rnorm(400 * p, sd = 0.2), nrow = 400, ncol = p)
  
  X <- Z %*% t(A) + eta
  
  y <- Z[, 1] + Z[, 2] + rnorm(400, sd = 0.5)
  
  X_train <- X[1:200, ]
  X_test <- X[201:400, ]
  
  y_train <- y[1:200]
  y_test <- y[201:400]
  
  for (i in seq_along(k_values)) {
    
    k <- k_values[i]
    
    knn_fit <- knn.reg(
      train = X_train,
      test = X_test,
      y = y_train,
      k = k
    )
    
    test_mse[i, j] <- mean((y_test - knn_fit$pred)^2)
  }
}

colnames(test_mse) <- c("m = 3", "m = 30")

data.frame(
  k = k_values,
  test_mse
)

  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The test MSEs for each value of k are shown in the table above. For m=3, the lowest test MSE was 0.4497 at k=10. For m=30, the lowest test MSE was 1.8238 at k=10.

After averaging the test MSE across 50 simulations, m=3 had a lower test MSE than m=30 for every value of k. For both values of m, the average test MSE was lowest around k=10 and then increased as k became larger.

Even though both settings have 100 observed predictors, the underlying dimension of the data is different. When m=3, most of the structure in the 100 predictors comes from only 3 latent variables. This makes it easier for KNN to find observations that are actually close to each other. When m=30, the data varies across many more latent dimensions, so distances become less informative and KNN has a harder time finding useful neighbors. This explains why the test MSE is much higher for m=30. The noise term η\eta also adds variation to each observed predictor, so the observations do not lie perfectly in an m-dimensional subspace, which makes finding close neighbors more difficult.

Solution: Question 4

Show the workflow 
zip_train <- read.csv(
  "data/knn/zip-train.csv.gz",
  header = FALSE
)

zip_test <- read.csv(
  "data/knn/zip-test.csv.gz",
  header = FALSE
)

X <- as.matrix(zip_train[1:1000, -1])
y <- zip_train[1:1000, 1]

X_test <- as.matrix(zip_test[1:500, -1])
y_test <- zip_test[1:500, 1]

euclidean_distance <- function(x0, X) {
  sqrt(rowSums((X - matrix(x0,
                           nrow = nrow(X),
                           ncol = ncol(X),
                           byrow = TRUE))^2))
}

manhattan_distance <- function(x0, X) {
  rowSums(abs(X - matrix(x0,
                         nrow = nrow(X),
                         ncol = ncol(X),
                         byrow = TRUE)))
}

knn_classify <- function(X, y, X_test, distance) {
  
  y_hat <- integer(nrow(X_test))
  
  for (i in 1:nrow(X_test)) {
    
    d <- distance(X_test[i, ], X)
    
    neighbors <- order(
      d,
      1:nrow(X)
    )[1:5]
    
    votes <- tabulate(
      y[neighbors] + 1,
      nbins = 10
    )
    
    y_hat[i] <- which.max(votes) - 1
  }
  
  y_hat
}

pred_euclidean <- knn_classify(
  X,
  y,
  X_test,
  euclidean_distance
)

pred_manhattan <- knn_classify(
  X,
  y,
  X_test,
  manhattan_distance
)

euclidean_errors <- sum(pred_euclidean != y_test)
manhattan_errors <- sum(pred_manhattan != y_test)

euclidean_errors

The 5NN classifier calculates the distance between each test observation and every training observation using either Euclidean or Manhattan distance. It then selects the five closest training observations and predicts the digit using a majority vote. If observations are tied in distance, the observation with the smaller training row number is selected first. If there is a tie in the majority vote, the smaller digit is predicted.

Using Euclidean distance, the 5NN classifier made 61 classification errors out of 500 test observations. Using Manhattan distance, the classifier made 69 errors. Therefore, Euclidean distance performed slightly better on this test set. The confusion matrices above show the classification results for each digit.

The three images above show examples that were incorrectly classified using Euclidean distance. Some of the digits have shapes that look similar to other digits, which can cause their nearest neighbors to belong to the wrong class. Overall, Euclidean distance performed slightly better than Manhattan distance, with 61 errors compared to 69. The two distance measures can produce different nearest neighbors because Euclidean distance uses the square root of the sum of squared differences between pixel values, while Manhattan distance uses the sum of absolute differences. For this dataset, Euclidean distance resulted in slightly better classification performance.

# STAT 432 Plot Formatting

- Keep the original data, calculations, and statistical meaning of the plot unchanged.

- Apply these formatting rules to existing R or Python plotting code without changing the underlying analysis.
